name: Imposter Syndrome Test
tagline: Do you feel like a fraud despite your achievements?
intro: This test explores four common sides of imposter feelings: doubting your abilities, fearing being found out, discounting your successes and overworking to compensate. Rate how much you agree with each statement, thinking of your work or studies. It takes about five minutes and shows you which imposter patterns are strongest for you.
seoTitle: Imposter Syndrome Test – Free online self-check
seoDescription: Do you feel like a fraud at work? Take this 5-minute test on self-doubt, fear of exposure, discounting and overworking. Get practical tips.

self_doubt.name: Self-doubt
self_doubt.short: How much you question your own skills and competence.
self_doubt.low: Your answers suggest you have a solid, realistic trust in your abilities. You seem to feel you belong in your role and can take on new challenges without heavy doubt. This confidence helps you learn and contribute. Keep it healthy by staying curious and asking for feedback, so your self-trust remains grounded in what you actually do well and where you can still grow.
self_doubt.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes question your abilities, especially in new or high-pressure situations. You probably feel confident in familiar tasks but less so when the stakes rise. Keep a simple record of skills you have used and problems you have solved. When doubt appears, look at the evidence rather than the feeling. Remind yourself that feeling unsure while learning is normal and does not mean you are not capable.
self_doubt.high: Your answers suggest that self-doubt is a strong theme for you. You may often feel less capable than the people around you, even when your results say otherwise. This can hold you back from speaking up or taking chances. Try writing down specific facts about your work, such as feedback, completed projects and skills, and read them when doubt hits. Talk with a mentor about how they see you. If self-doubt weighs on your wellbeing, a coach or qualified professional can help.

fear_of_exposure.name: Fear of exposure
fear_of_exposure.short: How much you fear being 'found out' as less capable than people think.
fear_of_exposure.low: Your answers suggest you rarely worry about being found out. You seem comfortable having your work reviewed and admitting what you do not know. This openness makes it easier to learn quickly and build trust with others. Keep modelling this attitude, for example by asking questions in meetings; it often helps colleagues who feel less secure feel more at ease too.
fear_of_exposure.mid: Your answers suggest that the fear of being exposed comes up now and then, perhaps around reviews, presentations or new roles. You may sometimes avoid questions to hide gaps in your knowledge. Try asking one genuine question each week in a safe setting and notice how people respond. Usually, curiosity is seen as a strength. Remember that nobody knows everything, including the people you admire.
fear_of_exposure.high: Your answers suggest you often worry that others will discover you are not as capable as they think. This fear can make reviews, questions and visibility feel threatening and can lead you to hide. Many highly capable people share this feeling. Try telling a trusted colleague or friend about it; saying it aloud often reduces its power. Practise admitting small gaps in knowledge openly. If this fear causes ongoing stress or anxiety, a qualified professional can help you work through it.

discounting.name: Discounting success
discounting.short: How much you play down your achievements and praise.
discounting.low: Your answers suggest you can recognise and own your achievements. You seem to accept praise and see a link between your efforts and your results. This is important for motivation and resilience. Keep taking a moment to acknowledge your wins, and also give credit to others where it is due; owning success and sharing it go well together. A balanced view of yourself is a solid base for growth.
discounting.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes play down your successes, perhaps calling them luck or saying the task was easy. Some modesty is fine, but too much can distort how you see yourself. Next time someone compliments you, try simply saying thank you without adding a correction. At the end of each week, write down one thing you did well and what skill made it possible.
discounting.high: Your answers suggest you often discount your achievements, explaining them away with luck, help from others or easy circumstances. Over time this can leave you feeling that nothing you do really counts. Start a success file with feedback, results and thank-you messages, and read it regularly. When you notice yourself explaining away a win, ask what role your own effort played. If this pattern affects your mood or self-esteem, a qualified professional can help you build a fairer view of yourself.

overworking.name: Overworking
overworking.short: How much you overprepare or overwork to prove you are good enough.
overworking.low: Your answers suggest you keep a healthy balance between effort and rest. You seem able to stop when work is good enough and to trust your preparation. This protects your energy and wellbeing. Continue to guard this balance during busy periods, and notice early if you start working late or skipping breaks to prove yourself. Rest is part of good performance, not a reward for it.
overworking.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes work harder or prepare more than needed to feel safe. This can bring good results, but it may cost more energy than necessary. Set a clear time limit for preparation and agree with yourself what good enough looks like before you begin. Plan at least one real break each day and treat it as part of doing your job well.
overworking.high: Your answers suggest you often overwork or overprepare to make sure no one sees a weakness. This may have helped you succeed, but it can lead to exhaustion and makes success feel fragile, as if it depends only on extra effort. Experiment with doing slightly less on a low-risk task and see what happens. Protect your sleep and free time. If overwork is affecting your health or relationships, please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional.

summary: Imposter feelings are very common, especially among capable, conscientious people. Below you see how strongly four imposter patterns show up in your answers. Higher scores mean the pattern is more present. Imposter syndrome is not a medical diagnosis, and this test is a tool for self-reflection.
